script.opening: “Hi. Um, first — I’m Rowan, not Rebecca, and I use they/them. The system still has my old name. I keep getting letters about a smear test. The last one went really badly, and honestly I’m not sure I even need one.”

facts.text: If asked: “Four years ago. The nurse kept calling me Rebecca and ‘young lady’ even after I told her. It really hurt and I asked her to stop. I left in tears and haven’t been back to a GP since, except online.”
“I’ve been on testosterone gel for eighteen months through the gender clinic. My periods mostly stopped after about four months.”

“I only had sex with women until this year — that’s partly why I thought I didn’t need a smear. Now I’m with Dev — he’s a man — four months.” Condoms: “Most of the time.” No other partners in the last year.

Only if asked about bleeding, or asked “is there anything else worrying you?”: “Actually, there’s something. I’ve bled after sex twice in the last couple of months. Just a bit of red. I didn’t know if it’s the testosterone. I’ve been worried.”
Last spotting 10 days ago. No bleeding at other times recently. No pelvic pain, no discharge, no pain during sex except some dryness. No weight loss, no fevers.
If asked: “I thought testosterone stopped you getting pregnant… doesn’t it?” Has not done a pregnancy test. Last unprotected sex about a week ago.
No medical problems. Non-smoker, alcohol occasionally. No allergies. HPV vaccine at school: “I think so.”

“I’d like my name changed to Rowan and the title Mx. I want my pronouns on there so I don’t have to keep saying it.” If asked about changing the gender marker: “I’ve thought about it. Would that change anything?”
If asked: “I’d want someone who gets it. Not rushed. Maybe I could put the speculum in myself? And I’d want to be able to stop.”

Guarded and a bit tense, watching how the doctor responds to your name and pronouns. If the doctor uses “Rebecca”, “she” or “Miss”, become curt and give short answers. If the doctor apologises for the past experience and uses your name and pronouns naturally, open up and mention the bleeding. Do not raise the bleeding until asked about bleeding or invited to share other worries. If told you need an examination, hesitate (“I really don’t want a repeat of last time”) and agree if adjustments are offered.

ice.ideas: Maybe they don’t need screening because they had sex mainly with women; maybe the bleeding is due to testosterone.
ice.concerns: Being misgendered and hurt again; something being wrong with the cervix; whether they could be pregnant.
ice.expectations: Records corrected, an honest answer about screening, and to be treated with respect.

cues: “The system still has my old name” — test of respect from the first minute.
“I left in tears” — the depth of the previous experience.
Pause before saying “I’m not sure I even need one” — the bleeding is behind it.

checkpoints.text: Uses the correct name and pronouns throughout and asks how they would like to be addressed
Takes a relevant history — screening history, testosterone use, sexual history and partners, contraception, bleeding pattern (postcoital, intermenstrual), pain and discharge
Identifies postcoital bleeding as needing clinical examination of the cervix and STI testing, and identifies the need for a pregnancy test
Explains screening eligibility accurately — anyone with a cervix aged 25–64; HPV passes between partners of any gender; testosterone does not remove the need

Plans an adapted in-person examination (chosen clinician, longer slot, smaller speculum, self-insertion, right to stop, consider vaginal oestrogen pre-treatment with the gender service) with STI tests and cervical sample if due; safety-net and follow-up
Advises that testosterone is not contraception and can harm a pregnancy; offers suitable options (progestogen-only methods, IUDs, condoms) and emergency contraception considerations
Acknowledges and apologises for the previous poor experience without defensiveness, and builds trust
Updates the record (name, title, pronouns) and explains how changing the registered gender marker affects automatic screening invitations, offering manual recall

worked.txt: “Thanks, Rowan — I’ll update that today. I’m sorry the record was wrong.”
“I’m really sorry about what happened last time. Being misgendered and hurt during an examination shouldn’t happen, and I can understand why you didn’t come back.”
“Screening is for anyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 who has ever been sexually active. HPV can pass between partners of any gender, so you do still need it.”
“Have you had any bleeding after sex, or between periods?”
“Bleeding after sex is usually from something harmless like dryness or an infection, but it does need someone to look at the cervix — a screening test alone isn’t enough.”
“Testosterone doesn’t reliably stop ovulation, so pregnancy is possible, and testosterone can harm a developing baby. Let’s do a pregnancy test and talk about contraception that works alongside it.”

f.learning: Inclusive care starts with the basics: use the person’s name and pronouns, correct the record, and acknowledge past harm. Anyone with a cervix aged 25–64 who has ever been sexually active should be offered cervical screening, whatever their gender or partners’ gender; trans men and non-binary people registered as male are not invited automatically, so practices must recall them manually. Testosterone can cause vaginal atrophy, making examination uncomfortable; a short course of vaginal oestrogen beforehand may help (discuss with the patient and gender service), along with a smaller speculum, self-insertion, a chosen clinician and an explicit right to stop. Postcoital bleeding is a symptom, not a screening question: examine the cervix, test for STIs, and refer on a suspected cancer pathway if the cervix looks suspicious. Testosterone is not a contraceptive and is teratogenic; offer progestogen-only methods, IUDs and condoms. From August 2026, HPV self-sampling kits are being offered to some under-screened people in England, but self-sampling is not suitable when there are symptoms.

wordPics.clearPass: Uses Rowan’s name and pronouns from the start, acknowledges past harm sincerely, explains screening eligibility accurately, uncovers the postcoital bleeding and pregnancy risk and manages them correctly (examination, STI tests, pregnancy test, contraception compatible with testosterone), plans a genuinely adapted examination, and updates the record with clear advice about gender marker and recall.
wordPics.pass: Respectful throughout; explains eligibility and plans an adapted screening appointment; identifies the bleeding and arranges examination, with contraception or record changes covered more briefly.
wordPics.fail: Respectful but focuses only on screening; misses the bleeding or pregnancy risk; or plans a standard smear without adaptations.
wordPics.clearFail: Misgenders repeatedly or uses the old name, tells them they do not need screening because of past partners or testosterone, or dismisses the bleeding; no plan.

avoid.dont: “As a woman, you still need your smear.”
avoid.instead: “Anyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 should be offered screening.”
avoid.why: Misgenders and alienates; use anatomy-based, neutral language.

avoid.dont: “If you’ve mostly had sex with women you probably don’t need it.”
avoid.instead: “HPV can pass between partners of any gender, so screening is still recommended.”
avoid.why: Inaccurate; under-screening in LGBTQ+ people is a recognised problem.

avoid.instead: “Testosterone isn’t reliable contraception and could harm a pregnancy.”

model.text: Hi Rowan, I’m Dr Clarke — I use he/him. Thanks for telling me your name and pronouns; I’ll update the record today. I’m sorry it was wrong. What would you like to talk about?
model.why: Uses correct name, models pronouns, commits to action

model.text: I keep getting smear letters. Last time went really badly. I’m not sure I even need one.
Can you tell me what happened last time?
The nurse kept calling me Rebecca and young lady, it hurt, I asked her to stop and left in tears.
I’m really sorry. That shouldn’t have happened, and it makes complete sense that you haven’t wanted to come back. If we plan anything, it will be on your terms, and you can stop at any point.
Can I ask a few health questions so I can give you the right advice? You’re on testosterone — how long, and what’s happened with periods? And who are your partners at the moment?
Eighteen months; periods stopped. I was only with women until this year — now Dev, he’s a man, four months.
Thanks. Have you had any bleeding after sex or between periods, pain, or discharge?
model.why: Asks directly about bleeding — uncovers the hidden concern

model.text: Actually… I’ve bled after sex twice in the last couple of months. I didn’t know if it was the testosterone.
I’m glad you told me. And for contraception — what do you and Dev use?
Condoms, mostly. I thought testosterone stops pregnancy anyway.

That’s a really common belief, but testosterone doesn’t reliably stop ovulation, and it can harm a developing baby. So a pregnancy test is sensible now. Options that work well alongside testosterone include the implant, the progestogen-only pill or a coil — and condoms protect against infections.
model.why: Corrects misconception; contraception compatible with testosterone

model.text: On screening: anyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 who has ever had sex should be offered it — HPV can pass between partners of any gender. The bleeding after sex is different: it’s usually something harmless like dryness or infection, but it needs someone to look at your cervix and do swabs, not just a screening test.
model.why: Accurate eligibility and correct approach to PCB

model.text: I really don’t want a repeat of last time.

Let’s design it with you. A longer appointment with a clinician experienced in trans and non-binary care, a smaller speculum, and you can insert it yourself if you prefer. Testosterone can make the tissues dry, so a short course of vaginal oestrogen beforehand may help — I’ll check with your gender team. We can take the screening sample at the same time as the swabs. And I’ll change your name to Rowan, your title to Mx, and add your pronouns. If you change your registered gender later, the automatic screening letters may stop, so we’d set up a reminder ourselves.
model.why: Adapted exam, liaison, records and recall

model.text: That actually sounds okay. Thank you.
Let’s book that within the next two weeks. If you get heavier bleeding, pain or discharge before then, or the pregnancy test is positive, contact us straight away.

knowledge.guideline: UKHSA/NHS England NHS population screening: information for trans and non-binary people (current) · NHS Cervical Screening Programme: 5-yearly interval for HPV-negative people aged 25–49 (from 1 July 2025) and HPV self-sampling offer for under-screened people (from August 2026) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, updated April 2026) · CoSRH Statement on contraceptive choices and sexual health for transgender and non-binary people (2017, updated) · GMC Good medical practice (2024) · Equality Act 2010
knowledge.summary: Offer cervical screening to anyone with a cervix aged 25–64, whatever their gender identity or partners. Use correct names and pronouns, adapt examinations, and treat symptoms such as postcoital bleeding as symptoms needing examination. Testosterone is not contraception.

points.t: Anyone with a cervix aged 25–64 who has ever been sexually active. People registered as female are invited automatically; those registered as male are not, so practices should recall manually.
In England, people aged 25–49 who test HPV-negative are recalled every 5 years (for tests from 1 July 2025); 50–64 every 5 years. HPV-positive results lead to earlier recall or colposcopy.

A symptom, not a screening issue: examine the cervix, test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, consider pregnancy. Refer on a suspected cancer pathway if the appearance of the cervix is consistent with cervical cancer; persistent unexplained PCB merits gynaecology referral.

Testosterone causes vaginal atrophy. Options: smaller speculum, lubricant, self-insertion, positioning, a short course of vaginal oestrogen beforehand (discuss with the gender service), longer slot, chosen clinician, right to stop.

Testosterone does not reliably suppress ovulation and is teratogenic. Suitable options: Cu-IUD, LNG-IUS, implant, progestogen-only pill or injection; condoms for STIs. Oestrogen-containing methods are usually avoided by preference and because they may counter masculinising effects.
HPV self-sampling kits are being offered to some under-screened people in England from August 2026. They are not suitable when someone has symptoms.
Name and title can be updated on request; record pronouns. Changing the registered gender marker can affect screening invitations (and may create a new NHS record); agree a manual recall plan.
Use the person’s name and pronouns; apologise for past harm; ask what would help. Discrimination on grounds of gender reassignment is unlawful under the Equality Act 2010.

social.t: Trans and non-binary people often avoid care after poor experiences, leading to under-screening and late presentation.

legal.t: Gender reassignment is a protected characteristic. Non-binary people should be treated with dignity and without discrimination; services should make reasonable adjustments.

professional.t: Treat patients fairly and with respect; use preferred names and pronouns; raise concerns about poor care and consider feedback to colleagues.

community.t: Jo’s Cervical Cancer Trust (information for trans and non-binary people), LGBT Foundation, Live Through This; local trans-inclusive sexual health clinics.

pitfalls.intro: The first 30 seconds decide this station. After that, the marks are in finding the bleeding and the pregnancy risk.

items.fail: Using the registered name or “she” from the notes.
items.why: Repeats the harm that drove them away.
items.fix: Use the name and pronouns they give; update the record.

items.why: Misses postcoital bleeding, which needs examination.
items.fix: Always ask about bleeding after sex or between periods.
